headline: The JavaScript 3D Library That Grew Into a Rendering Engine
lede: Three.js, the open-source 3D rendering library that has shaped the visual web since 2010, shipped release r184 in April 2026. The update added a visual node-graph shader editor, an upsampling algorithm ported from PC gaming, and live HTML-to-texture rendering — prompting one observer to ask whether 'library' still describes what Three.js actually is. The question deserves a careful answer.
body:
Three.js began in 2009 as a personal project by Ricardo Cabello, known online as mrdoob, who ported his own Flash graphics code to JavaScript. When Firefox 4 brought *WebGL* to consumer browsers in 2011, the project found its purpose. Today it claims 2,000 contributors and five million weekly downloads on *npm*, making it by some distance the most widely used 3D rendering package on the web.

What r184 adds illuminates the tension the poster identified. The headline item is a *TSL Graph* pane inside Three.js's own Inspector: a visual, node-based shader editor that ships inside the repository, not as a third-party plugin. Alongside it: `FSR1Node`, a JavaScript port of Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD) **FidelityFX Super Resolution** upsampling algorithm; `TAAUNode`, *temporal anti-aliasing with upsampling*; a `LightProbeGrid` for position-dependent *global illumination* — the simulation of indirect light bouncing between surfaces; and `HTMLTexture`, which renders live HTML as a 3D surface. A *NodeMaterial* compatibility layer now bridges the old per-shader *GLSL* system to the new node-based one, a convergence underway since roughly 2021.

The case for calling Three.js an engine rests on cumulative scope. It ships a visual scene editor, a devtools panel with memory profiling and a command timeline recorder, and *TSL* — the Three.js Shading Language — a JavaScript-native abstraction that compiles to GLSL or *WGSL* at runtime and includes thirty-odd built-in *post-processing* effect nodes. A parallel *WebGPU* renderer has been production-ready since r171, coinciding with Apple's Safari on iOS joining the WebGPU-capable browser roster in September 2025. *WebXR* support for VR and AR is built in. Physics wrappers for Rapier and Jolt live inside the official repository. No third-party vendor is required for any of it.

The counterargument is precise. Three.js still ships no native physics engine — the bundled wrappers delegate to external libraries. There is no game loop, no *entity-component system*, no audio pipeline, no GUI toolkit. Babylon.js and PlayCanvas both include most of those. Cabello has resisted the drift toward completeness deliberately; the core stays minimal, and orchestration belongs to the user. The result resists easy categorization: a **rendering engine** with editor-grade tooling, but not a game engine in the sense Epic Games' Unreal Engine or Unity Technologies (U) defines the term.

The practical consequence is that ambitious Three.js applications still require assembly — picking a physics library, wiring a game loop, handling audio separately. But the rendering core those pieces plug into now carries feature ambitions that sit alongside commercial engines. Whether Cabello's project deserves a new name is a semantic argument; whether the gap to full-engine status is closing by design or by drift is not.

concepts.definition: A browser API that exposes GPU-accelerated 3D graphics to JavaScript, based on OpenGL ES. It has been the foundation of Three.js since 2011 and remains the primary rendering path for most deployed applications today.
The Node Package Manager — the default package registry for the JavaScript ecosystem. A library's weekly download count on npm is a standard proxy for real-world adoption across production projects.

A JavaScript-native abstraction for writing GPU shaders that compiles to either GLSL (for WebGL) or WGSL (for WebGPU) at runtime. It replaces the painful practice of manually splicing GLSL strings and allows a single shader codebase to target both rendering backends without rewriting.

OpenGL Shading Language — the C-like language historically used to write GPU programs (shaders) for WebGL. GLSL files describe how geometry is transformed in space and how individual pixels are colored on the GPU.
WebGPU Shading Language — the shader language for the WebGPU API. It is stricter and more structured than GLSL and cannot be used interchangeably with it without a transpilation layer like TSL.

The next-generation browser graphics API that succeeds WebGL. It exposes lower-level GPU control — including compute shaders and explicit render pipelines — and became universally available across major desktop and mobile browsers, including Safari on iOS, in late 2025.

An upsampling algorithm from Advanced Micro Devices that renders a scene at a lower internal resolution and reconstructs a higher-resolution image using spatial filtering. Originally designed for PC gaming to improve frame rates, Three.js r184 ported it as a *post-processing* node.

A rendering technique that accumulates pixel information across multiple consecutive frames to simultaneously reduce aliasing (jagged edges on geometry) and upscale the output image. Unlike purely spatial methods, TAAU improves in quality the longer a scene remains static.

A class of rendering techniques that simulate how light bounces between surfaces — so a red wall faintly tints a nearby white ceiling, for instance. Accurate global illumination is computationally expensive and was historically confined to offline renderers or high-end game engines.

A material system where shading logic is defined as a graph of interconnected nodes — each node performing one operation — rather than as raw shader code. It offers composability, cross-backend portability, and visual editability, and is the foundation of TSL in Three.js.

A pipeline of image-space effects applied after the main 3D scene has been rendered to a texture: bloom, depth of field, color grading, ambient occlusion, film grain, and similar. Post-processing runs entirely on the GPU and treats the rendered frame as an input.

The browser API for VR (virtual reality) and AR (augmented reality) experiences. It standardises device discovery, head-tracking, controller input, and stereoscopic rendering — Three.js ships WebXR support without requiring additional libraries.

An architectural pattern common in game engines where game objects (entities) are bare identifiers, behaviour is attached through components (data structs), and systems process all entities that match a given component signature. ECS prioritises performance and flexibility but requires more structural setup than a simpler object hierarchy.

repos.summary: The canonical Three.js repository, maintained by mrdoob and roughly 2,000 contributors under an MIT licence. It contains the renderer, the visual editor, TSL, the Inspector devtools, physics wrappers, and hundreds of bundled examples — the full scope of what the project has accumulated since 2010, all in one place.

fact_check: The poster's claim that Three.js 'is an engine' holds on the rendering axis — it ships a scene editor, devtools, a cross-backend shading language, and a WebGPU renderer — but overstates the case if taken to mean a full game engine. Three.js has no native physics engine, no game loop, no entity-component system, and no audio system, all of which Babylon.js and PlayCanvas include as standard. The more precise characterisation is rendering engine, not game engine.
